segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: If you really love something, maybe a sport or a hobby, a music band or a TV show, you

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: might call yourself a fan.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Nowadays, thanks to the internet, fans from around the world can meet online to share their

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: their passion. And this has led to a new word fandom. Fandom is more than simply being a fan.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: It's a whole culture created by a community of people to share their love of the same thing.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: What's more, fandom has started to develop its own language. In this programme, we'll be taking

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: a trip into the world of fandoms and, as usual, we'll be learning some new and useful vocabulary

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: too. But before that, I have a question for you, Neil. The original word fan was first used about

segments.speaker: Beth

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: a. Hollywood movie stars, b. Baseball or c. Disney cartoons?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I'll guess they were fans of Disney cartoons.

segments.speaker: Michael Bond
segments.text: Kings rule their kingdoms fans certainly rule their fandoms It taps into that ancient human impulse to belong to a group of like people

segments.speaker: Michael Bond
segments.text: And of course, being a fan by yourself can be a challenging thing

segments.speaker: Michael Bond
segments.text: because fannish pursuits can look quirky and odd.

segments.speaker: Michael Bond
segments.text: Or even obsessive, I suppose.

segments.speaker: Michael Bond

segments.text: I mean, if you're a Jane Austen fan and you want to dress up in a bonnet and gown of the Regency era,

segments.speaker: Michael Bond
segments.text: it's difficult to do that by yourself in public.

segments.speaker: Michael Bond
segments.text: But once you join a fandom, there's no problem.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Fans are groups of like-minded people.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: They share similar opinions, ideas or interests.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: They do all kinds of weird and wonderful things together,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: such as dressing up as Harry Potter characters,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: behaviour which might be called quirky an adjective meaning odd or unusual, but in an interesting way.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Unfortunately, this quirky behaviour also means fans sometimes get mocked.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: To mock somebody means to insult them by laughing at them in an unkind way.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But this hasn't discouraged fans who have started using new words and phrases to show they belong to a particular fandom.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here's Michael Bond again, explaining the meaning of two new words about the behaviour of football fans to BBC Radio 4 programme Word of Mouth.

segments.speaker: Michael Bond
segments.text: Academics who study fandoms they love to use acronyms and abbreviations And they got several phrases which they use to describe the behaviour of football fans And berging So that means basking in reflected glory

segments.text: Oh, I love that.

segments.text: When your team wins, everyone wants a bit of the action.

segments.speaker: Michael Bond

segments.text: And so the sort of antithesis of that is a core thing, which means cutting off reflected failure.

segments.text: And that is what people sometimes do when their team loses and they don't want to be associated with that loss, that sense of failure.
